note.explanation: Data is raw facts collected about things around us. It can be processed to make useful information. Data may be numbers, words, measurements, observations, images, or sounds, and can come from different sources.
examples: Weather data includes temperature, humidity, and wind speed collected from weather stations.
A store may record the number of products sold and their prices.
note.checkAnswer: Data consists of raw facts collected about things around us that we can process to generate useful information.
note.simple: Data is unprocessed information we collect. When we work with it, it can help us understand something or make a decision.

written.text: What is the difference between qualitative and quantitative data?
written.finalAnswer: Qualitative data describes qualities or categories, usually in words; quantitative data is numerical and can be counted or measured.

written.text: Explain the differences between qualitative and quantitative data. Provide examples of each type.
written.finalAnswer: Qualitative data describes qualities or categories, usually in words; an example is favourite ice cream flavour. Quantitative data is numerical and can be counted or measured; examples include a temperature reading or the number of students in a class.

explain.title: Data means raw facts
explain.body: Data consists of raw facts collected about things around us that we can process to generate useful information.

explain.title: Data comes in many forms
explain.body: Data can be numbers, words, measurements, observations, images, or sounds. It may come from different sources.

explain.title: Examples of data
explain.body: Weather stations collect measurements such as temperature, humidity, and wind speed. Stores record sales, websites record visitor activity, and surveys collect responses.

explain.title: Why data matters
explain.body: Understanding data helps us comprehend situations, make informed decisions, solve problems, and drive innovation. For example, analysing weather data can help scientists issue early storm warnings.

mistakes: Calling data only numbers: the section also includes words, measurements, observations, images, and sounds.
Confusing raw data with useful information: data can be processed to generate useful information.
Giving an example without connecting it to its source or what it records.
